evidence.section_title: 'The self-destruction force is so strong': male survivors' experience of suicidal thoughts following sexual violence
evidence.quote: The purpose of this study was to explore the experience of male survivors themselves of suicidal thoughts following sexual violence within the framework of men and masculinity.

evidence.section_title: Introduction
evidence.quote: The purpose of this study was to increase knowledge and deepen understanding in this area by exploring the experience of male survivors themselves of suicidal thoughts following sexual violence within a theoretical framework of men and masculinity.

evidence.section_title: Method
evidence.quote: In this study, interviews were conducted with seven male sexual violence survivors who had experienced suicidal thoughts following the violence

evidence.section_title: Ethical considerations
evidence.quote: The research question of the study, 'what is the experience of male sexual violence survivors of suicidal ideation following sexual violence?', guided the selection of the sample. Purposive sampling (five participants) and snowball sampling (two participants) were used, and thus, seven participants selected who had experienced suicidal thoughts following sexual violence.

evidence.section_title: 'The self-destruction force is so strong': male survivors' experience of suicidal thoughts following sexual violence
evidence.quote: The research methodology was The Vancouver School of Doing Phenomenology, and a total of 17 interviews were conducted with seven male survivors.

evidence.section_title: Method
evidence.quote: In this study, interviews were conducted with seven male sexual violence survivors who had experienced suicidal thoughts following the violence, two interviews with four of them and three interviews with three, a total of 17 interviews. The first author, and primary researcher, conducted all the interviews.

evidence.section_title: Author contributions
evidence.quote: EDVT collected the data, did the primary data analysis and drafted the manuscript.

evidence.section_title: 'The self-destruction force is so strong': male survivors' experience of suicidal thoughts following sexual violence
evidence.quote: The main findings of the study are that the source of the suicidal thoughts after sexual violence is based on an experienced strong self-destruction force that involves almost unbearable and unexpressed suffering. The strong self-destruction force appeared among other things in risk behaviour and negligence towards own life and health. Participants all agreed that the thought of suicide was a certain escape route, that is to be constantly trying to escape from oneself and inner suffering. Negative thoughts that were difficult to suppress developed into suicidal thoughts that developed into thinking about the best possible way to commit suicide. Shattered self-esteem, shame and loneliness characterised the lives of participants, and they felt disgusting and worthless as human beings. Much self-degradation was characteristic. Perceived common societal norms about male masculinity had major negative impact on participants, for example that they should not show emotions because they were men and therefore should not express emotional pain or disclose their traumas. This resulted in emotional silencing. Disclosing the violence proved extremely difficult for all participants, but they experienced a high level of positive energy following disclosure.

evidence.section_title: Results
evidence.quote: ['suicidal thoughts following sexual violence are based on an experienced \'strong self-destruction force\' that involves almost unbearable suffering which is still unexpressed but primarily focused on avoiding frequent thoughts about the violence and finding peace.', 'The strong self-destruction force resulted in participants\' risk behaviour, such as driving too fast without seatbelts, high drinking and consumption of other drugs to kill the emotional pain, as well as total indifference to their own health and life.', 'Discussions in society about sexual violence could increase their suicidal ideation.', 'Much stress also resulted in more suicidal ideation.', 'They were so used to thinking of death that it became part of everyday life.', 'Destructive thoughts, lack of selfesteem and loneliness characterised their life and hopelessness were common.', 'They felt they were bad and worthless human beings and talked about disconnection of body and mind.', 'Common societal norms about male sexual violence survivors had a major negative impact on all participants.', 'The most common was the masculine image of the strong silent man who should not express any emotional pain which had a very negative effect on their emotional life and involved a certain emotional silencing.', 'A common myth the men were dealing with was that men cannot be raped by a woman which prevented their disclosure about such violence.', 'They also reported the fear that they would themselves become perpetrators, or be judged as such, as they felt that myth was strong in society.', 'Disclosing the violence proved extremely difficult for them, but they experienced a high level of positive energy after disclosure.', 'The reaction of others mattered, and trauma-specific support was very important to them.']

evidence.section_title: To quit the plan to commit suicide: 'I did not want to leave my boy'
evidence.quote: When suicidal thoughts had developed into planning the suicide, the participants stopped the planning because they did not want to leave family members behind. Ian said he had organised the suicide and thought carefully about the method. He recounted, 'You start to wonder, for example about family members'. Henry said he had planned to jump from a balcony. He said, 'I think I was standing there for perhaps an hour when I decided not to give up, I did not want to, I did not want to leave my boy'. David talked about feeling better and better as he organised his suicide in more detail. He attended to all loose ends so that nothing would become a burden on those left behind and felt calmer. After attaining some resulting peace, he decided not to go through with the plan.

evidence.section_title: Disclosure: 'It's a great positive energy that gushes forth following disclosure'
evidence.quote: [/page/6/Text/11] Disclosure was a huge step for all the participants, whether it was with a partner, friend, expert, counsellor or others. When they finally disclosed what had happened, they experienced great positive energy and a new sense of freedom. Some participants experienced valuable support from their loved ones while others would have liked more emotional support. It seemed that the most valuable support came from male buddies who had been through the same experience.

evidence.section_title: Physical manifestation of emotional sufferings: 'Mind and body hold hands'
evidence.quote: All participants struggled with health problems and mentioned unexplained pain and other physical symptoms they believed were related to the sexual violence. Emil said he did not have a strong connection with his body, was unhappy with it and had an unusually high pain threshold. Liam said he had suffered from severe abdominal pain, which he said was related to the violence. David has fibromyalgia and was convinced that it was related to the violence. Jonah said: I sometimes get twitches during the day [...] I cannot trace this directly to the trauma, but it all started at that time. After working on my mental problems, the twitches have diminished.

evidence.section_title: Looking for help: 'I did not know that I could get help there – being a man'
evidence.quote: All participants have sought assistance in dealing with their trauma, to psychologists, psychiatrists or centres for victims of sexual violence. Initially, when they wanted to seek help, they were not aware that they could go to counselling centres for sexual violence survivors, being men. Later, they found out that help for them was available and they found great help. Ian felt it was important to always have the same counsellor as he did not want to tell his story all over again. He also mentioned that he enjoyed meeting his adviser and to just talk with him about everyday things and thus not always be talking about the violence. Most of them experienced the emergence of a new world when getting appropriate traumaspecific help.

evidence.section_title: The freedom found in disclosure
evidence.quote: [/page/7/Text/10] Their conclusion is that disclosure is a difficult and complex process and male stereotypes have created such an environment for men that disclosure is hard for them. Alaggia and Mishna (32) found in their study that male survivors find it hard to disclose violence, among other things, because they find it difficult to regard themselves as victims, especially in the case of sexual violence. We found this in the cases where women were the perpetrators. Men's difficulties regarding disclosure can also be linked to the social belief that sexual violence rarely happens to boys and it complicates matters further, and even becomes a taboo to talk about, when victims and perpetrators are of the same sex (33). Furthermore, men who report violence often face disbelief and diminishment and are, therefore, very reluctant to disclose, and thus, the risk of the violence lasting longer increases, the perpetrators will keep on violating boys and men, and some victims will probably never disclose (33). [...] In our study, the men experienced an intense relief when they did disclose their trauma. Trauma-specific support was important for them and the most valuable support came from fellow male survivors.
